newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark 1998 fiscal tightening about 0.5 pct GDP -finmin.
newsitem.headline: Denmark 1998 fiscal tightening about 0.5 pct GDP -finmin.

text.p: Danish Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft said on Tuesday that he would maintain a stringent fiscal policy in 1998, with tightening of around the level of 1996 and 1997's 0.5 percent of Gross Domestic Product.

"I'm not in a position to tell you exactly which tools we will use, but I can assure you that the budget we will present in August will contain a negative fiscal effect," he said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
"I think we will continue around the area we had before, in the region of 0.5 percent," he added.
Danish central bank governor Bodil Nyboe Andersen called last week for "appreciable" tightening in 1998 to prevent the economy from overheating.
Latest finance ministry estimates indicate that, despite the budgeted 0.5 percent tightening, the actual effect in 1996 was a 0.2 percent easing.
In Tuesday's interview, Lykketoft said that the ministry's December forecast of 2.7 percent inflation for 1997 was still on course.
He said he expected his minority government to win broad parliamentary support for a tight budget, despite its dependence on the far left to pass the 1997 finance bill.
"There is a growing understanding of the need to maintain the stability of the Danish economy," he said.

He added that although there was broad political support for Danish membership of Economic and Monetary Union, the need for a new public referendum on the issue meant that it was unlikely to be in the first wave of members if the January 1999 schedule is maintained.
"Nobody expects a new referendum to take place early enough to join at the beginning but most think there will be a referendum at some point. I think so too," he said.
Denmark is one of the few European Union members already meeting the economic performance criteria for membership of EMU but is bound by a binding 1993 referendum vote to stay out.
A reversal of that decision requires a fresh plebiscite.

Lykketoft doubted that French President Jacques Chirac's decision to dissolve parliament and set snap elections for May-June risked upsetting the EMU schedule if Chirac's centre-right coalition were to lose to the rival Socialists.
"I don't think so, I don't hope so. For any French government it is very essential that this happens according to the timetable, on January 1999," he said.
Lykketoft denied rumours that his Social Democrats planned to call a Danish election before the present coalition government's term expires in September 1998.
"My opinion is that our wish is to continue to the very end," he said. --Copenhagen newsroom +45 33 969650
